title: Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas)
summary: Cross-service atomicity is hard. Two-phase commit coordinates strong atomicity at high cost; sagas use sequenced local transactions with compensations for practical workflows.

sections.title: 2PC mechanics
paragraphs: Prepare then commit. Blocking on coordinator failure is the classic weakness. XA works in narrow environments; across microservices and heterogeneous stores it is painful.

sections.title: Sagas
paragraphs: Each step commits locally; on failure, run compensations. Orchestration vs choreography styles. Idempotency is mandatory.

sections.title: Outbox pairing
paragraphs: Transactional outbox starts reliable saga messages. Without it, dual writes reopen the original consistency hole.

sections.title: Choosing
paragraphs: Prefer single-service transactions when possible. Use sagas for long business workflows. Reserve 2PC for tightly controlled homogeneous systems.

deepDive.title: Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas) intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

keyTakeaways: Avoid distributed tx when you can
whyItMatters: Microservices without a transaction story create inconsistent business state.
reflectionQuestions: What is the compensation for each step in your checkout flow?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
